sections.title: A cabin for the weekend
sections.body:
Narrator: You will hear a traveller arranging a cabin holiday with a booking clerk. Look at the booking form and listen for the arrangements that the speakers finally agree on.

Mira: My sister recommended the cabins on your country park website. On the map I can see a campsite by the lake with a wooden platform. Is that where we would stay?

Nora: The lakeside site only takes tents. Our cabins are at Willow Bend. There is a separate footpath to the lake, so you can still visit the platform without walking on the road.

Mira: That sounds better with the children. I was hoping to arrive on Friday the eighteenth of April. Will the cabins be open by then?

Nora: They will be open, but a school group has booked Friday night. The first night I can offer is Saturday. You could arrive before lunch and leave the family bags with us while the cleaner finishes.

Mira: Let us have three nights from then. We can come home on Tuesday. There will be two adults, my daughter who is ten and my nephew who is five. He is young but he sleeps in an ordinary bed.

Nora: The cabin called Otter sleeps three. For four people I would reserve Heron. It has a small bedroom with bunk beds and a double in the living room. Eagle has another double but is much farther from the play area.

Mira: Heron, please. Your price list has two different figures under family cabins. Could you explain what we actually pay when we book?

Nora: The April rate is sixty pounds per cabin per night, including bedding and heating. We take a deposit of forty pounds now. The balance is due a week before the visit.

Mira: Do I need to pack washing-up liquid or extra sheets? My sister mentioned something she had to buy when she forgot to bring it.

Nora: There are sheets on the beds and a bottle by the sink. The thing to bring is towels. People often arrive expecting bath towels because we supply the rest of the linen.

Mira: We are arriving by train. Someone thought all the buses outside the station went past the park. Is it just a matter of taking the first one?

Nora: No. The blue bus turns inland at the village square. Take the green bus outside the station. Get off at Old Mill. That stop is much closer when you are walking with young children and luggage.

Mira: And if we run late? I see the reception desk closes at six. I do not want to make the trip and then find we are locked out.

Nora: After six you collect the key at the café. It stays open until nine. The code on your letter opens the gate, which is separate from the cabin key. Phone the duty worker if you will reach us even later.

Mira: My daughter heard about an evening activity with a telescope. Can I ask the receptionist about it when we arrive?

Nora: The telescope event is full. There are still places on the Sunday night walk, but you must book it online. The ranger prints her list before leaving the office, so reception cannot add anyone.

Mira: I will do that tonight. I can give you my email address now. Should I print the entire booking letter before the visit?

Nora: A printout is optional. Please save the confirmation number on your phone. The signal is poor by the gate and that number is all we need to look up the booking.

sections.title: A guide to Harbour Yard
sections.body:
Narrator: You will hear a volunteer introducing a riverside craft centre. Look at the map. North is at the top, and the main gate is on the south edge.

Jo: Welcome to Harbour Yard. The first building on your left as you enter, in the south-west corner, is the repair workshop. The table outside looks like a café table, but it is where apprentices receive damaged items for an estimate.

Jo: Across the path from the workshop there is an old sign above a door. It still says ticket office, although we sell tickets online now. The tool library is on your right just inside the gate. Go there to borrow a drill.

Jo: Carry on towards the river and you will find a bench at the crossroads. Turn left and walk towards our red brick building. The gallery is in the north-west corner. Its wide doors date from when it was a loading hall.

Jo: The last building is our classroom. An early Wednesday group meets there each week. The session is for people who need a quieter visit. We switch off the demonstration tools and limit the group size. It costs the same as the afternoon session.

Jo: Our volunteers run two demonstrations this morning. The first uses a wooden boat frame. The usual teacher is away, so it begins at eleven thirty rather than eleven. The second demonstration starts at the time printed on your ticket.

Jo: To handle the boat frame you must wear an apron. There are clean ones hanging outside the room, and gloves are ready at the benches. If you choose just to watch, you can keep your ordinary clothes on.

Jo: Keep cameras in bags while people work. A visitor stepping backwards for a photograph could trip over a bench. You are welcome to photograph the finished pieces in the gallery once the practical session is over.

Jo: The shop sells small objects made here. We used to wrap purchases automatically; now you can ask at the desk for paper. The money from sales pays for school visits. It covers travel for classes that could not otherwise reach us.

Jo: We also collect unused hand tools. First send us a photograph by email. If we can use the tool, we will send you a delivery date. Please wait for that reply instead of leaving a box outside the gate on a wet morning.

Jo: Check the noticeboard as you leave. On the last Sunday of the month we close an hour earlier for a fire drill. Today is the second Sunday, so you have the full afternoon. Pick up a calendar at the entrance for a reminder.

sections.title: Designing a study of lecture notes
sections.body:
Narrator: You will hear two education students discussing how to compare handwritten and typed lecture notes. Both will take responsibility for different aspects of their project.

Ana: I read your outline. Do you want to find out which group records more words? A person typing might easily win that competition without making particularly useful notes.

Ben: Exactly. Our main question is how well students understand the lecture. Counting words alone would say very little about whether the typist understood the argument.

Ana: You drafted an invitation for the whole university. Could previous knowledge account for the differences between groups? A third-year student might have encountered the topic in another class.

Ben: Let us recruit first-year students from the same course. They will have had similar teaching so far. We still cannot assume that everyone knows exactly the same amount, of course.

Ana: For the initial check I would ask four questions about background knowledge. Ask them before explaining how the two groups will differ. Otherwise people might try to guess which group we want them to join.

Ben: Could we let them choose the way they normally take notes? Nobody would be stuck with a method they dislike, and it would be easy to explain.

Ana: People choosing laptops might already have special skills. Allocate the methods by drawing lots. With enough participants, each person has the same chance of ending up in either group.

Ben: I booked two different rooms to keep keyboard noise away from the handwriting group. But does our budget allow us to pay the lecturer twice?

Ana: Record the lecture once. Play the same recording in both rooms. That prevents a longer example or a joke in one room from affecting the outcome. The room bookings will still be useful.

Ben: Shall we divide the jobs? I can edit the recording. You already have experience of writing question papers. Our tutor offered to look at the first draft.

Ana: Yes, I will write the test. Put me down as the person responsible for the assessment materials. The tutor is happy to advise but cannot write the items for us.

Ben: I will also check the sound balance. Last time I made a recording it was hard to hear questions from the back row. We will use a microphone this time and test it before recording the lecture.

Ana: The tutor agreed to store the consent forms in her locked cabinet. We will put numbers on our spreadsheets and use those during marking. Neither of us will need access to the names while the study is running.

Ben: When participants take the final test, are we testing pure memory? Some classmates felt we should take the paper and the laptops away before asking anyone a question.

Ana: Let participants use their notes. Their ability to use the record they made is what interests us. If we take notes away, memory becomes more important than the note-taking method.

Ben: I will schedule a small pilot. Its purpose is to check the instructions. I do not want people waiting at the start because they are unsure whether diagrams are allowed. We can change any unclear wording before the main trial.

sections.title: How walls store summer heat
sections.body:
Narrator: You will hear an introductory lecture on heat storage. The lecturer describes an experiment and refers to the cross-section of a model room.

Lecturer: A wall can be warm long after sunset. To see how a wall stores heat we built two model rooms. In one a brick formed the front wall. In the other we used light board. We changed only the front wall. The roof, floor and other sides were identical.

Lecturer: You might expect us to put the models outdoors. In fact we heated the walls with a lamp. A passing cloud would have changed the outdoor conditions part way through the measurements. We needed an exposure that we could repeat the next day.

Lecturer: Look at the cross-section from left to right. The sloping shape represents the lamp. The black square marked A touches the outside of the wall. This is the surface sensor. A second instrument is suspended inside the room, away from the floor and the wall.

Lecturer: At B, the suspended instrument measures the air rather than the building material. We call it the air probe. It has a shield to prevent the lamp warming the instrument directly without changing the temperature of the air.

Lecturer: The two instruments send readings along the cables to the box at C. This box is a data logger. Because it uses one clock for both instruments, we can compare the moment the outside became warm with the moment a change was detected inside.

Lecturer: Before switching on the lamp the class made predictions. Some expected brick to warm the room faster because it felt cold when touched. In fact the air in the board model warmed first. The change in conditions outside had reached its inside air sooner.

Lecturer: When we switched off the lamp, the board model started cooling. Inside the brick model, however, the temperature continued to rise briefly. We call the delay between the outer and inner temperature peaks the time lag. It shows that the movement of heat takes time.

Lecturer: It would be wrong to assume that a brick room is always cooler. During several hot days in a row, the wall needs to lose some heat at night. In the follow-up trial we opened two vents after dark. Cool air flowing through them carried heat away.

Lecturer: One difficulty was that the air outside the models varied during the night, particularly when somebody left the classroom door open. Next time I would record the classroom temperature too. This would show how much opportunity the model really had to lose heat.

Lecturer: Finally, the models are simpler than a real house. Our models have no windows. Sunlight coming through glass can add heat directly to the inside, independently of what the wall is doing. We plan to add that feature before we investigate a full-size building.

sections.title: Booking a bicycle repair course
sections.body:
Narrator: You will hear a customer speaking with a worker at a community bicycle workshop. Listen for the details of the course that the customer chooses.

Sam: My aunt gave me an old bicycle. Is the class called Road Ready suitable for someone who has never taken a wheel off?

Ruth: Road Ready assumes a little experience. What you want is First Repairs. It begins with the names of the tools and goes slowly enough for people who have used bicycles for years without touching the brakes.

Sam: The workshop meets on Saturday or Wednesday according to the website. I work in a shop on Saturdays. Are there spaces left on both days?

Ruth: Saturday is full anyway. Wednesday has one space left. It runs in the evening so there is no conflict with a day shift. You do not have to join the waiting list for the other group.

Sam: Does it begin at six? I usually get home at about that time but I could come straight from work and stop for something to eat afterwards.

Ruth: We open at six. Teaching starts at six thirty. Come before the teaching begins so that you have time to set up your bicycle. The session finishes at eight, with time to catch the bus home.

Sam: I rode past the door with a wheel painted on it. It faces a very busy street. Will we have to carry our bicycles up the steps there?

Ruth: The painted door leads to the shop. For classes, enter through the courtyard. That route takes you to the back of the building, where you can wheel your bicycle all the way to the bench.

Sam: My neighbour offered me a toolbox, but it is rather heavy. Is there any point trying to carry all of it on the bicycle?

Ruth: We provide every tool you need. Please bring a notebook. There is a diagram in the handout, but many people like to write down the adjustments they have made on their own bikes.

Sam: If a part is badly damaged would you still accept the bicycle for class? I cannot judge whether the frame is safe.

Ruth: We check the frames first. If yours is unsafe, we lend you a practice bicycle. We would not sell you replacement parts before establishing that the frame itself can be used.

Sam: The list price is eighty pounds. I no longer qualify for the student discount because I finished university last term. Do you offer any other reductions?

Ruth: With proof of a local address your total is sixty pounds. That covers all four sessions. There is no further reduction for bringing somebody else, although we can put a friend on the waiting list.

Sam: I have a library card and a bank letter on my phone. Which one would you prefer to see when I arrive for the first class?

Ruth: Bring the bank letter. Some library cards do not show an address. A digital version of the letter is acceptable if both your name and address can be seen on the screen.

Ruth: Yes, we send a payment link. If you have to miss a session, tell us by email. We can send the worksheet to you, but there are no places on the other course for people wanting to make up an evening.

Ruth: Yes. The tutor saves the last fifteen minutes for questions. I can also put a note on your form so she knows about your brake noise before the class begins. I will send the payment link this afternoon.

sections.title: Inside the new community centre
sections.body:
Narrator: You will hear the centre manager welcoming visitors to a building. Look at the ground-floor plan. The main entrance is at the bottom, and a straight corridor runs from the entrance to the garden at the top.

Grace: If you stand just inside the entrance, the first room on your right is the kitchen. It serves the evening cookery club. On winter afternoons you can smell the bread long before you get to the main door.

Grace: On the left of the entrance is the office. We originally considered putting it at the far end to give staff a quieter working space. Visitors often have an immediate question though, and that is why it stayed near the entrance.

Grace: Follow the corridor all the way to the garden doors. The last room on your left is the music studio. The walls by the garden were easier to insulate. A group can rehearse there without interrupting a meeting in the office.

Grace: Across from the studio is the hall. The lines on its floor mark table positions for different events. We keep the tables downstairs but the projector is upstairs. Anybody arranging a film night should ask a member of staff to bring it down.

Grace: A group from the neighbourhood pays a reduced price. A charity from farther away pays the usual price. The local rate depends on where the group is based. It makes no difference how many people attend, or whether the event raises money.

Grace: To request a room, first check the shared calendar. A white square means the time is free. A grey square means we are reviewing an earlier application, so you should choose a white slot rather than waiting for a grey square to change.

Grace: Once you have picked a slot, send a description of your event. The form has a box for the title too, but a title alone is not enough. We check the description to see if the room will suit your equipment.

Grace: Wait until the office sends confirmation before advertising. We sometimes get a lovely poster on a Monday morning for an event we cannot actually fit in. Receiving confirmation first saves a great deal of wasted printing.

Grace: At a public meeting, drinks must be served in reusable cups. We have enough for seventy people. The same rule applies if you order your refreshments from a café, so mention the rule when you place your order.

Grace: During normal hours return the key to the office. After hours use the metal box beside the side door. Only the duty manager can empty it. Do not drop keys through the letter slot at the front because they would land on the public side of the desk.

sections.title: Planning a museum label trial
sections.body:
Narrator: You will hear two design students discussing how to evaluate written labels at their local museum. Listen to their decisions about the sample, measurements and reporting.

Nina: The curator offered us paintings, musical instruments and a case of domestic tools. I thought pictures would be best because people often spend longer looking at them.

Lee: I considered paintings too, but they have recorded commentary. The tools have no commentary. That makes it easier to tell whether visitors learned something by looking at a written label.

Nina: We have two labels for each object, one with a paragraph and another arranged as a list. Can we avoid letting visitors simply read the same words twice?

Lee: Only show each person one version per object. Use lists for half the objects and paragraphs for the others. The next morning swap the versions. Over the whole study every object will appear with both types.

Nina: Would a list with fewer words be fairer? Six short entries could be quick to read, especially for people visiting the museum with young children.

Lee: Then we would change two things at once. Keep the word count identical. That way any difference we find is more likely to be linked to the layout. We should keep the print size the same as well.

Nina: Someone suggested finding volunteers through the museum mailing list. Subscribers probably know the collection well, so the labels might appear clearer than they really are.

Lee: Recruit them at the door. Ask every fourth adult who comes in. That is better than only asking people who look willing to talk. If someone declines, record that and begin the count again.

Nina: I have written down the purpose of each measure. Time spent at the case is a measure of attention. A long visit could mean interest or confusion, so time alone is a poor measure of what someone understood.

Lee: Questions at the exit measure recall. They ask what a particular tool was used for. We will be measuring immediate recall because we have no arrangements to contact the same people a week later.

Nina: The coloured cards indicate preference. Visitors drop a card in one of two boxes to show which layout they would like elsewhere in the museum. We can display both styles after the recall questions have been answered.

Lee: A group of friends could discuss a label and remind each other of the answer before reaching us. It would be unreasonable to stop all conversation during a museum visit.

Nina: Ask whether they discussed an object. Keep those answers and mark them separately. Removing them would give a misleading picture because many real visitors arrive with somebody else.

Lee: Our tutor can attend a pilot on Tuesday, but it is a public holiday. The crowded entrance hall may bear little resemblance to a normal day.

Nina: The best day for the pilot is Thursday. The school tour was moved to Friday, so we can use the entrance. I will ask the tutor to read our forms before Wednesday evening.

Lee: In the final report, include copies of the labels in an appendix. A reader would struggle to judge a layout comparison from words alone. We can reproduce our own labels there with the curator's permission.

sections.title: Measuring the quiet side of a city block
sections.body:
Narrator: You will hear a lecture about a small field study of urban sound. The lecturer describes how the investigators compared the street side and courtyard side of several buildings.

Lecturer: A street can sound busy while a courtyard a few steps away feels remarkably quiet. Our aim was to compare the two sides of the same building. We selected buildings with a street entrance on one side and a courtyard on the other. This paired approach made each building its own comparison.

Lecturer: We first considered working only in the morning to avoid interruptions from deliveries. A morning measurement, however, might not reflect conditions when residents returned from work. We decided to measure in three periods: morning, afternoon and evening. Each site received visits in every period.

Lecturer: Using a meter by the street and then carrying it through to the courtyard would have been easy, but a passing bus might have disappeared between readings. We used two meters simultaneously. In this way a sudden event happened at the same instant for both instruments.

Lecturer: The first practical step each morning was to inspect the batteries. Then the two meters were placed side by side beside a steady sound source. We compared their readings before separating them. A large disagreement at this stage would indicate an equipment problem.

Lecturer: Once the meters were in position, we avoided putting them directly against a wall. A hard surface could reflect sound back towards a sensor. We also fixed both sensors at the same height, using stands rather than expecting two people to hold them perfectly still.

Lecturer: Every observer kept a written log of unusual events. On one afternoon a delivery van stood with its engine running beside the street meter. The log did not give us a reason to discard the whole day. It allowed us to explain a short rise in the street readings.

Lecturer: The average street reading was higher at every building. But the largest difference occurred at the building with a closed passage. Its courtyard was connected to the street by a passage with a heavy door at each end. At sites with broad open arches the difference was smaller.

Lecturer: Some interviewees said they liked a courtyard even when its meter reading was quite high. Listen to their explanations: they mentioned birds and the voices of children. The type of sound mattered to those residents as well as its level. The meter could measure level but it could not measure preference.

Lecturer: We deliberately excluded rainy periods because droplets hitting the protective cover produced a sound of their own. This choice made interpretation simpler. It also meant we could not say whether our comparison held in wet weather, an important limitation in a city with frequent rain.

Lecturer: For the next study, I would add sound diaries kept by residents. People could describe what they heard at moments that mattered to them, including events outside our scheduled visits. We could then compare these accounts with the instrument records instead of assuming that the highest reading was always the most disturbing.
